tldr: This framework repurposes the rendering pipeline of sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR)—which represent 3D scenes in high detail—directly for collision probability computation. It pairs theoretical risk upper-bound guarantees with sub-millisecond GPU collision checking and gradient-based trajectory optimization.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Collision Rendering framework. Spherical cameras coinciding with collision spheres enclosing the robot render opacity, which—augmented with a theoretical error bound—serves for collision checking (green). The same rendering pipeline provides gradients used to optimize trajectories away from obstacles (blue, yellow).
overview:
Recently, radiance field techniques such as NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have made it possible to build extremely high-fidelity 3D spatial models directly from camera images. However, applying them to robot trajectory planning has hit a major barrier: the ambiguous safety criterion of where learned densities or Gaussians should actually count as obstacles. Prior works either relied on arbitrary empirical thresholds or spent considerable time converting fields into alternative map representations for a specific robot geometry, failing to reconcile theoretical safety guarantees with computational efficiency.

To tackle this, the authors turned their attention to Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields (SVR), which possess a structured voxel hierarchy. Approximating the robot as a collection of collision spheres and placing an omnidirectional "spherical camera" at the center of each sphere yields a brilliant insight: the ray opacity computed by SVR's GPU rendering pipeline acts directly as a fast numerical approximator of directional collision probability. Furthermore, by evaluating an upper bound on density gradients within voxels (the Lipschitz constant), they mathematically bounded the approximation error from discrete sampling. This yields "risk-bounded collision checking" that guarantees the collision probability stays below a user-specified risk tolerance.

This approach requires no conversion to secondary map formats and uses the learned SVR representation directly. It achieves blisteringly fast processing times of around 0.1 to 0.4 milliseconds per check on a consumer-grade GPU (RTX 5080) and seamlessly integrates trajectory optimization using rendering pipeline derivatives. Validations in simulation and with real-world drones confirm that it reliably generates collision-free, smooth flight trajectories across all evaluated queries.
contributions: Proposed a GPU collision checker that directly uses the rendering pipeline of learned sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR) without converting to other maps, guaranteeing a theoretical upper bound (risk-boundedness) on collision probability.
Analytically computed spatial gradients of collision costs through the same GPU rendering pipeline, enabling direct integration with standard trajectory optimization methods.
Integrated sampling-based path planning and gradient-based trajectory optimization, demonstrating 100% collision-free motion planning on a real-world drone flight and a 6-DoF robotic arm.

sections.heading: Can we fly robots safely directly inside high-fidelity maps built from images?
sections.summary: While radiance fields are promising high-fidelity 3D representations, balancing computational speed with reliable collision criteria required for trajectory planning has remained difficult. This paper observes that SVR's GPU rendering pipeline serves as an excellent collision probability approximator, offering theoretically guaranteed collision checking alongside differentiable trajectory optimization.
sections.details:
Safe trajectory planning is essential for robots to navigate real-world environments autonomously. Traditional sampling-based planning methods like RRT and PRM rely on occupancy grids, polygon meshes, or signed distance fields (SDFs). However, these depend on LiDAR or depth-camera resolution constraints and struggle to capture delicate structures such as thin wires or slender foliage.

Recently, radiance field methods like NeRF and 3DGS have drawn significant attention for reconstructing 3D scenes from sets of camera images. Among them, Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields (SVR) store density and color within an octree-based voxel grid. Unlike 3DGS, which suffers from density ambiguity due to overlapping primitives, SVR provides a structured, well-behaved representation.

Even so, using radiance fields for trajectory planning remains underexplored. There is no agreed-upon standard for how much density constitutes a collision, forcing prior works to rely on empirical thresholds or heavy, robot-specific preprocessing. The core discovery of this work is that placing a "virtual spherical camera" at each collision sphere enclosing the robot turns SVR rendering itself into an equivalent calculation of collision probability. This allows GPU-accelerated collision checking with safety guarantees in milliseconds, without any conversion or auxiliary representations.

sections.heading: How does this fundamentally differ from existing NeRF and 3DGS attempts?
sections.summary: Previous radiance-field-based trajectory planners (NeRF-Nav, CATNIPS, Splat-Nav, Splanning) suffered from heuristic thresholding, heavy geometry-dependent preprocessing, or degraded representation accuracy. This method modifies nothing about the learned representation and derives theoretical safety bounds directly.
sections.details:
### II-A Trajectory Planning on Radiance Fields
There are four notable prior works that plan trajectories on radiance fields:
- NeRF-Nav: Uses raw density from a learned NeRF as a collision penalty during optimization, but the penalty is not calibrated as a probability and carries no theoretical safety guarantee.
- CATNIPS: Treats the density field as a Poisson point process to derive exact collision probabilities, but convolves the density field with a robot-geometry kernel, requiring full map recalculations whenever the robot's size or configuration changes.
- Splat-Nav: Performs geometric interference checks against 3DGS Gaussian ellipsoids, but relies on empirical choices such as setting the collision boundary to 1-sigma.
- Splanning: Normalizes 3DGS to derive collision probabilities, but this normalization harms the underlying geometric and visual reconstruction fidelity, while its closed-form approximations end up overly conservative.

In contrast, the proposed method uses the "learned SVR model directly without modification," eliminates robot-geometry-dependent preprocessing, and derives mathematically provable upper bounds.

### II-B Comparison with Traditional Map Representations
Collision checking libraries (such as FCL) using geometric maps like OctoMap, meshes, or SDFs are mature. However, converting SVR into these formats introduces false checks from thresholding and loses fine details during marching cubes. As shown later in experiments, these conversion-based baselines fall significantly short of the proposed method in terms of safety.

sections.heading: Viewing light transmittance as non-collision probability
sections.summary: This section outlines the SVR data structure and volume rendering principles, connecting ray transmittance—the probability of a ray passing through without hitting particles—to the non-collision probability of an infinitesimal robot segment. Setting up an omnidirectional spherical camera model aligned with the collision sphere forms the theoretical foundation.
sections.details:
### III-B Fundamentals of Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields (SVR)
In SVRaster, which forms the basis of this work, space is adaptively partitioned with an octree, and raw density values $Z$ are stored at the 8 vertices of each voxel. Density inside a voxel is computed via trilinear interpolation followed by an activation function $\sigma = \operatorname{explin}(Z)$. Because adjacent voxels share vertex values, the density field is spatially continuous.

### III-C Collision Criteria in Density Fields
In volume rendering, ray transmittance across an interval $[t_a, t_b]$, given by $T(t_a \to t_b) = \exp(-\int_{t_a}^{t_b} \sigma dt)$, represents the probability that light traverses the interval without interacting with particles. Here, the authors introduce Assumption 1: this transmittance can be interpreted as the probability that an infinitely thin rigid rod along that line segment does not collide. Therefore, for a collision sphere of radius $R$ centered at $\mathbf{p}$, the directional collision probability along direction $\mathbf{d}$, $P_{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}; R)$, is the complement of transmittance, $1 - T(0 \to R)$. The sphere's overall collision probability is then defined as the maximum across all directions: $\max_{\mathbf{d}} P_{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}; R)$.

### III-D Spherical Camera Model
To evaluate this collision probability via GPU rendering, an omnidirectional $360^\circ$ spherical camera is placed at the collision sphere's center $\mathbf{p}$, rather than a pinhole camera. The ray direction $\mathbf{d}$ is determined from pixel coordinates $(x,y)$, and ray-box intersections and alpha-blending proceed just like in standard SVR renderers. Through this, rendered pixel opacity $A$ directly corresponds to collision probability.

captions.F2: Correspondence between SVR rendering structure and collision probability. (a) Density sampling and opacity computation inside voxels, (b) transmittance $T$ in a continuous density field, and (c) the fundamental assumption equating ray transmittance from the collision sphere's center outward to the non-collision probability of a rigid rod.

sections.heading: The full algorithm: A duet between sampling search and differentiable optimization
sections.summary: The proposed system consists of two modules: a risk-bounded collision checker and a differentiable collision cost gradient evaluator. After global search (A* or RRT) identifies a rough safe path, local optimization using opacity gradients refines it into a smooth trajectory kept comfortably clear of obstacles.
sections.details:
The workflow of the proposed method is very straightforward.

First, the robot's geometry is modeled as the union of $M$ collision spheres. A spherical camera is placed at each sphere center $\mathbf{p}_m(\mathbf{q})$.

1. **Collision Checker (Algorithm 1)**:
For each collision sphere, a spherical opacity image is rendered on the GPU. If the maximum rendered opacity $A_{\max}$ exceeds the risk tolerance $\tau_c$, a collision is declared immediately. Only if it is below the threshold does the system evaluate the theoretical upper bound $A^{\mathrm{ub}}$, which adds the error bound $\varepsilon$ described later. If $A^{\mathrm{ub}} < \tau_c$ holds across all spheres, the state is verified safe. This two-tier check bypasses redundant calculations while fully guaranteeing safety.

2. **Trajectory Optimizer (Algorithm 2)**:
For each waypoint along the initial path generated by a sampling-based planner, a slightly larger "optimization sphere" of radius $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ is assigned. A collision cost is computed from the opacity image rendered by this sphere, and its spatial gradient with respect to the sphere center is evaluated analytically on the GPU. Backpropagating this gradient through the Jacobian into joint or configuration space allows gradient descent—combined with trajectory smoothness task costs—to push the trajectory away from obstacles. Because updated candidate trajectories are validated by the collision checker at every step, safety is preserved even if optimization terminates early.

sections.heading: Taming rendering errors: The math behind theoretical safety upper bounds
sections.summary: Rendered opacity is merely an approximation produced by discrete sampling. By deriving a Lipschitz constant for density from trilinear interpolation within voxels, the authors bound both ray-wise discretization errors and angular gaps between pixels, arriving at an upper-bound formula that never underestimates true collision probability.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Why Simple Integration Fails and Assumptions
In SVR, raw density $Z$ varies as a cubic polynomial inside a voxel and enters the exponent via the $\operatorname{explin}$ activation function. Consequently, ray integrals cannot be solved analytically in terms of elementary functions (Liouville's theorem). Numerical integration is therefore unavoidable, meaning the approximation error must be strictly bounded from above to provide safety guarantees.

### V-C Two Types of Approximation Errors
Spherical opacity rendering incurs two error sources:
1. **Ray error**: Numerical integration error caused by sampling a finite number of points (midpoint samples) along the ray.
2. **Angular error**: The risk of missing features in the gaps between rays where no ray passed.

### V-D Deriving the Sphere-Wise Upper Bound
Using the differences across the 8 voxel vertices, the authors analytically derived the maximum rate of density variation along a ray (the Lipschitz constant $L_{\mathrm{ray}}$). This bounds the ray error $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ray}}$ proportionally to the square of the sample step $h$.
Furthermore, by partitioning the angular cone centered on a pixel into radial shells, they derived an angular error bound $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ang}}$ using the maximum gradient $G_{b,j}$ of neighboring voxels.

Combining these into a total error bound $\varepsilon_b$ yields an upper bound $A^{\mathrm{ub}}$ on the true collision probability from pixel opacity $A_b$:
$$A^{\mathrm{ub}} = \max_b \left[ 1 - (1 - A_b) \exp(-\varepsilon_b) \right]$$
If this value is below the specified risk tolerance $\tau_c$, directional collision risk is mathematically guaranteed to stay below $\tau_c$ along every infinitesimal segment in all directions. This entire computation is implemented as a few-line CUDA kernel within SVR's existing rendering pipeline, running blisteringly fast.

captions.F3: Two error sources in the collision probability upper bound. (a) Integration error along the ray due to discrete sampling ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ray}}$), and (b) angular error from missing voxels situated between neighboring rays ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ang}}$), both mathematically bounded using Lipschitz constants.

sections.heading: Differentiating opacity to generate repulsive forces away from obstacles
sections.summary: By treating rendered opacity images as collision costs, the authors analytically derived spatial gradients with respect to the sphere center. Closed-form gradient computation accounting for ray integration and moving voxel boundaries allows GPU-parallel calculation of repulsive vectors that steer trajectories away from obstacles.
sections.details:
### VI-A Derivation of Rendering Opacity Gradients
How does rendered opacity $A_b$ change when a collision (or optimization) sphere moves slightly? Shifting the center $\mathbf{p}$ induces two effects:
- Density shifts at each sample point due to the translation of the ray origin.
- Expansion or contraction of the ray-voxel intersection interval (entry and exit distances $t^{\mathrm{in}}, t^{\mathrm{out}}$).

Applying fundamental calculus principles, the authors derived clean, closed-form gradient formulas (Theorem 2 and Corollary 1) separated into terms for moving boundary intersections and terms for internal density gradients. Because gradients for each pixel can be computed independently, they are fully parallelized on the GPU just like standard rendering.

### VI-B Trajectory Optimization Process
At each waypoint of the initial path, an optimization sphere with a radius $R_{\mathrm{o}}$ slightly larger than the robot's collision sphere is placed. Using an oversized sphere is deliberate: collision spheres on an initial collision-free path may already be far enough from obstacles that their opacity is near zero, yielding no gradient. A larger sphere captures surrounding obstacles, creating a repulsive force that establishes a wider clearance margin.

The collision cost $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{coll}}$, formed by averaging the highest rendered opacities, is combined with a smoothness cost $\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{task}}$ in gradient descent. Every candidate trajectory update is verified by the risk-bounded collision checker, ensuring that safety is strictly maintained even if optimization is halted at an arbitrary step.

sections.heading: Impressive safety and speed: From simulation to real-world drone flights
sections.summary: Evaluated against existing radiance field planners and geometric map conversion baselines across synthetic and complex photorealistic scenes, the proposed method achieved zero undetected collisions (0% FNR) with minimal false alarms (FPR), delivered 100% collision-free trajectories across all 80 benchmark queries, and successfully completed real-world autonomous drone flights.
sections.details:
### VII-A Setup and Environments
Experiments were conducted on a workstation with an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU. Baselines included four radiance field methods (NeRF-Nav, CATNIPS, Splat-Nav, Splanning) and two conventional geometric representations converted from SVR (OctoMap and triangular meshes).

### VII-B Checker Sensitivity and False Negatives
Collision checking against ground-truth meshes was evaluated over a grid in a synthetic environment with randomized objects (Table I, Fig. 4).
- The proposed method achieved a 0% false-negative rate (FNR) while keeping its false-positive rate (FPR)—falsely flagging safe areas as collisions—down to 4.640%.
- While CATNIPS (FPR 11.431%), Splat-Nav (12.254%), and Splanning (12.908%) also attained 0% FNR, their FPR was 6.8 to 8.3 percentage points higher than the proposed method, meaning they over-conservatively rule out large navigable areas. Mesh conversions and NeRF-Nav missed over 16–20% of actual collisions.

### VII-C Mobile Robot Planning Performance
Mobile robot trajectories were planned across four environments: Forest, Pavilion, Statues, and Stonehenge (20 queries each, 80 total; Tables III–VII).
- **Success Rate**: Only the proposed method achieved 100% collision-free trajectories across all environments and queries. CATNIPS achieved 100% on Statues but dropped to 65% in the densely foliated Forest, while NeRF-Nav managed only 20–65%.
- **Planning and Preprocessing Time**: Proposed search and optimization took 0.400–0.880 s on average (under 1 s). Baselines required 4.5–22.6 s of map preprocessing (e.g., PURR construction, polytope extraction), whereas the proposed method requires zero preprocessing.
- **Query Latency**: A single collision check took just 0.078–0.387 ms, demonstrating remarkable responsiveness on the GPU.

### VII-D Ablation Study
Comparing trajectories planned with and without the collision cost confirmed that opacity-gradient optimization increased minimum obstacle clearance with statistical significance ($p < 0.01$) across all environments, automatically steering trajectories toward wider safety margins (Table VIII).

### VII-E Real-World Drone Demonstration
Using an SVR reconstructed from smartphone images of an office room, flight trials were performed with a Crazyflie 2.1 micro-quadrotor (Fig. 7). Out of 68 planned queries, 61 generated safe trajectories (89.7%, with failures due to conservative bounds near capture boundaries). During actual flight, the drone reliably completed its paths while smoothly avoiding cardboard obstacles.

captions.F4: Trade-off curve of collision detection performance (FNR vs. FPR) in synthetic environments. At the zero false-negative operating point (0% FNR), the proposed method (Ours) achieves a substantially lower false-positive rate (FPR) than prior methods such as CATNIPS and Splat-Nav.
captions.F7: Experimental results of autonomous real-world drone flights. (a) Planned trajectories in an SVR reconstructed from smartphone images, (b) Crazyflie 2.1 navigating around real obstacles under motion capture, and (c) breakdown of success and failure across 68 queries.

sections.heading: Extending to articulated arms and understanding theoretical boundaries
sections.summary: Beyond single-sphere mobile robots, the method readily extends to a 6-DoF manipulator (UR10e) modeled with 17 collision spheres, achieving high success rates. However, theoretical guarantees apply as directional bounds, leaving challenges such as joint continuous-time trajectory certification and scaling to higher sphere counts.
sections.details:
### VIII-A Extension to Articulated Robotic Arms
Because the proposed collision checker is modular, it integrates directly into robotic arm motion planning. Modeling a 6-DoF UR10e arm with 17 collision spheres along its links, the authors hooked it into OMPL's RRT-Connect to solve shelf-picking tasks (out-in and in-out-in; Table IX, Fig. 8).
Across 50 trials, 3DGS-based Splanning got trapped in local minima and attained only 42–64% success, whereas the proposed method reached 98% and 100% success with zero collisions. Nonetheless, planning time scales with the number of spheres, leaving room for further efficiency improvements on multi-link arms.

### VIII-B What the Collision Bound Guarantees—and What It Does Not
From a theoretical standpoint, the method guarantees an upper bound on individual directional collision risks (an individual chance constraint), not the joint probability of a collision occurring somewhere across the entire sphere. Because neighboring rays encounter shared obstacles, assuming independence fails, and formulating the joint probability requires knowing microscopic particle scales that cannot be identified from image radiance fields.
Furthermore, the bound applies at discretely sampled configurations; continuous-time safety between waypoints relies on sufficiently fine resolution, as in standard sampling planners. In practice, however, the method sustained a perfect record of zero mesh collisions across all experiments, proving to be an exceptionally robust safety metric.

captions.F8: Motion planning results for a UR10e articulated arm in a shelf environment. On narrow shelf traversal tasks (out-in and in-out-in), collision checking with 17 spheres produces collision-free, smooth arm trajectories.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A harmonious marriage of graphics rendering and robot planning
sections.summary: By redefining SVR's GPU rendering pipeline as a collision probability approximator, Collision Rendering achieves theoretically guaranteed fast collision checking and gradient-based trajectory optimization. This marks a significant step forward for accurate, safe real-world robotics directly using radiance fields.
sections.details:
This paper introduced Collision Rendering, a trajectory planning framework that uses the rendering pipeline of learned Sparse Voxel Radiance Fields (SVR) directly as a numerical collision probability calculator.

By leveraging voxel Lipschitz continuity to bound numerical errors, the system evaluates theoretical collision risk bounds on a GPU in sub-milliseconds, while also deriving analytical opacity gradients to guide trajectory optimization. This eliminates both the ad-hoc thresholds and time-consuming map conversions that plagued earlier radiance-field planning methods.

Simulations, real-world drone flights, and robotic arm experiments demonstrated superior collision avoidance and execution speed compared to prior art. Promising future directions include bounding joint collision probabilities over full spheres and continuous trajectories, enabling end-to-end trajectory optimization in arm configuration spaces, and optimizing parallel performance when dealing with many collision spheres.

takeaways: Repurposing a standard computer graphics rendering pipeline as a robotic collision probability calculator is both remarkably elegant and practical.
Leveraging SVR's regular octree voxel structure and trilinear interpolation enables rigorous, Lipschitz-based upper-bound (risk-bound) error evaluation.
Planning directly on learned weights of high-fidelity radiance fields reconstructed from images—without lossy conversions to meshes or OctoMaps—is vastly superior in both safety and speed.
limitations: The theoretical guarantee bounds individual directional collision risks from the sphere center, rather than the joint probability of collision across the entire sphere or robot body.
Guarantees apply only to discretely checked configurations; continuous-time certification over swept volumes between waypoints remains an open challenge.
For articulated manipulators requiring many collision spheres, the number of render passes scales with sphere count, increasing planning time linearly.
